title: Shop Bill
context: Grade 3, the last working topic of the money chapter. An adult sees sums on money, which a toy shop and a handful of dummy notes and coins do well. What is being settled is which sum a question is asking for: the cost of many is the price of one taken many times, the cost of one is the whole amount shared out, a bill is the cost of each line and then every line added, and enough is the purse set against the price. A child who divides when the question asks for the cost of many, because the numbers are big, will get an answer that is smaller than the price of one and not notice. A child who adds the price of one to the count in a bill will total the wrong things.

writeup.why: Find the cost of many things by multiplying the price of one, share money equally by dividing, write a bill with the cost of each line and the total, and say whether the money in a purse is enough and by how much.
writeup.look: A shop counter with a shelf and an amber price tag, a sky blue count box, a tray of money and a row of plates, a bill table with a green total, a purse and a price tag on a balance, a words card under them, the Times, Share, Bill and Purse buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Shop Bill' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many things have been priced. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain shop counter fills the working area. The shelf stands at x 110, y 230, 560 by 230, and holds a row of at most nine of one kind of thing, each drawn large enough to count, such as pencil boxes, with an amber price tag hanging at its left end that reads the price of one. The sky blue count box sits at x 110, y 480, 190 by 70, with a plus and a minus, and a sky blue bracket under the row reads how many. The Times button stands at x 330, y 480, 150 by 70 and lays one copy of the price tag under every thing. The tray of money stands at x 700, y 230, 330 by 110, above a row of at most six plates at x 700, y 360, each drawn large enough to hold a small pile of flat notes and discs, with the Plates box at x 700, y 480, 190 by 70. In the Bill view the bill replaces the shelf, at x 110, y 216, 960 by 300: a table of four columns headed Thing, How many, Price of one and Cost, at most three lines, a rule under the last line and a green Total below it. In the Purse view the balance stands across the working area with the purse of notes and coins on its left pan at x 160, y 300 and the price tag on its right pan at x 700, y 300, and the gap is lit green when the balance has tipped. The words card stands under the shelf at x 110, y 566, 960 by 90, and says the step in writing, such as the price of one times how many. The Times, Share, Bill and Purse buttons stand in a row at x 110, y 666, each 150 by 60, labelled in words. A green Answer tag at x 700, y 480, 330 by 70, holds what the child has typed. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the cost, the share, the total or the difference into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag and a label. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. A note is a plain flat rectangle in its own colour and a coin a plain round disc, each with its value in large near-black type, so a value is read from the number and never from the colour. Anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because an amount is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The shop shows the last thing worked out, with the words card saying the step aloud and in writing and the green Answer tag beside it.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, as the count goes up, the price tag is copied once under every new thing and the cost under the row counts up one price at a time. On the fourth phase, when the child has typed the difference, the balance settles level with a soft click as the gap is made up by the missing money, or the extra money lifts out of the purse and rests beside it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a shelf of one kind of thing stands at the left with an amber price tag on it and a sky blue count box beside it, and the Answer tag is empty. On the second a tray of money stands above a row of empty plates, with a plus and a minus for the plates. On the third a bill lies on the counter with its lines of the thing, how many and the price of one filled in and every cost left empty. On the fourth a purse of notes and coins stands on one pan of a balance and a price tag on the other. One thing moves, once: the price tag gives one slow swing while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on a button is the whole way in.

voiceLines: A shelf of things with price tags, and a purse waiting on the counter.
Look at the price of one. How many will you buy?
Share the money so that every plate gets the same.
Find the cost of each line. Then find the total.
Count the money in the purse. Is it enough for the price?
A new shelf. What will you find out first?

observations.why: the cost of many is the price of one taken as many times as there are things.
observations.soWhat: to find the cost of many, multiply the price of one by how many.
observations.observe: As the count went up by one, the price tag was laid out once more and the cost grew by the same step.

observations.why: sharing equally gives every plate the same, so the whole amount is divided by the plates.
observations.soWhat: to share money equally, or to find the cost of one, divide the money by the number.
observations.observe: When the money was dealt out, every plate ended with the same pile and the tray was empty.

observations.why: the cost of a line is the price of one times how many, and the total is every line added.
observations.soWhat: find the cost of each line first, then add the lines for the total.
observations.observe: Each line of the bill got its own cost first, and only then were the costs added into the total.

observations.why: the side with more money weighs more, and the gap between them is the difference.
observations.soWhat: count the purse, compare it with the price, and the difference is what is left or still needed.
observations.observe: The balance tipped to the purse when it held more than the price, and to the price when it held less.

source_tool.description: A small shop counter fills the working area. A shelf at the left holds one kind of thing, such as a row of pencil boxes, with an amber price tag hanging from it that reads the price of one, and a sky blue count box beside it with a plus and a minus. The count sets how many things stand in the row, and a bracket under them reads how many. A Times button lays the price tag out once for every thing in the row, and a green Answer tag holds the cost the child has typed. A Share button opens a tray of money above a row of empty plates, and a plus and a minus set how many plates; the money is dealt out onto the plates one note or coin at a time until every plate holds the same. A Bill button swaps the shelf for a bill on the counter: a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, one line for each thing, with a rule under the last line and a green Total below it. A Purse button stands a purse of notes and coins on one pan of a balance and a price tag on the other, and the balance tips to the side that has more. In the tasks the shop is a snack stall, a stationery stall, a toy shelf, a fruit stall or a school fair. A words card under the shelf says each step aloud and in writing. The number pad types the cost, the share, the total and the difference. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many things have been priced.
source_tool.art_direction: A little shop counter / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Money is drawn as plain flat shapes: a note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin a round disc, each with its value in large near-black type. There is no portrait, no emblem, no serial number and no small print on any note or coin, because a child reads the value from the number. The notes are Rs 500, Rs 200, Rs 100, Rs 50, Rs 20 and Rs 10, and the coins Rs 20, Rs 10, Rs 5, Rs 2 and Rs 1. A note is always longer than it is tall and a coin is always round.

Real everyday things hold the money and the prices: a purse, a money box, a shop shelf with a price tag on each thing, a bill on a counter, a school fair stall. The object is the thing the child counts, pays or reads, and a bare column of figures appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

An amount is always written Rs 25.50: Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then exactly two digits of paise. Rs 5 and 5 paise is Rs 5.05, and a single digit of paise after the dot is never written. A whole number of rupees may be written without the dot, as Rs 36, or with two zeros, as Rs 36.00.

In a column sum the dots stand in one straight line, rupees to the left of it and paise to the right, with a heading Rupees over one part and Paise over the other. A carry or a borrow of one rupee is written small above the rupees column and its hundred paise above the paise column.
A price is a tag on the thing it belongs to. A bill is a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under the last line and the total below.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a note, a coin, an amount or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a note keeps its own colour, a coin its own metal, a purse its own leather. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag, a label and a typed answer, because the dot between them is the one mark that tells a child which part is which. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Rupees, Paise, Value, How many and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the price of one again. Ask what the question wants, and try once more.
voice.onNext: A new shelf. What will you find out first?
voice.opening: A shelf of things with price tags, and a purse waiting on the counter.
voice.onFinish: You worked out every price and every bill by yourself.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any price and any count, and watch what happens.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A bill: the cost of each thing and the total

placement.where: After the class has played the shop game with dummy notes and coins and priced a few things on paper, and before any sum is written on the board. The tool is what lets the price of one repeat as the count grows and lets an amount be dealt out until the plates are level, which a written sum alone does not show.

answer_key.rule: To find the cost of many things, multiply the price of one by how many. To share money equally, or to find the cost of one from the cost of many, divide the money by the number of things. A bill has one line for each thing, the cost of a line is the price of one times how many, and the total is every line added. The money in a purse is the notes and coins counted together. It is enough when it is the price or more. When it is more, the difference is left over, and when it is less, the difference is still needed. The answer is a number of rupees and Rs goes before it.
answer_key.wrong: The shelf is shown again with the price tag laid out once for every thing in the row, each one lit in turn and the costs counted up, or the money is dealt out again plate by plate while the plates fill level. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The price of one ticket is Rs 32.
We want 5 tickets, so we multiply the price of one by how many.
Rs 32 times 5 is Rs 160 in all.
5 tickets cost Rs 160. Rs goes before the answer.
items.question: A zoo ticket costs Rs 32. What do 5 tickets cost?
items.checkpoint: To find the cost of many, multiply the price of one by how many.
items.misconception: Adding the price and the count, Rs 32 and 5, and getting Rs 37.

steps: Sharing equally means every friend gets the same, so we divide.
Rs 216 divided by 6 is Rs 36 for each friend.
Check it by sharing back: Rs 36 times 6 is Rs 216 in all.
items.question: Rs 216 is shared equally by 6 friends. How much does each friend get?
items.checkpoint: To share money equally, divide the money by the number of friends.
items.misconception: Multiplying Rs 216 by 6 because the numbers are big.

steps: First find the cost of each line.
Line 1: Rs 9 times 4 is Rs 36 for the balloons.
Line 2: Rs 44 times 2 is Rs 88 for the caps.
Then add the lines. Rs 36 plus Rs 88 is Rs 124 so far.
Rs 124 plus Rs 33 is Rs 157 in all.
items.question: A party shop bill has 3 lines. 4 balloons cost Rs 9 each. 2 caps cost Rs 44 each. 1 mask costs Rs 33. What is the total?
items.checkpoint: Find the cost of each line first, then add the lines for the total.
items.misconception: Adding the prices of one, Rs 9 and Rs 44 and Rs 33, and forgetting how many of each.

steps: 2 notes of Rs 20 make Rs 40 together. 3 coins of Rs 2 make Rs 6 together.
Rs 200 plus Rs 40 is Rs 240 so far. Rs 240 plus Rs 6 is Rs 246 in all.
Now compare it with the price. Rs 246 minus Rs 239 is Rs 7 left over.
The money is more than the price, so it is enough.
items.answer: Yes. The money is Rs 246 and the rope costs Rs 239, so Rs 7 is left.
items.question: A child has 1 note of Rs 200, 2 notes of Rs 20 and 3 coins of Rs 2. A skipping rope costs Rs 239. Is there enough money? How much is left?
items.checkpoint: Count the purse, then compare it with the price to see which is more.
items.misconception: Saying the money is not enough because the note of Rs 200 is less than the price.

items.question: A sticker sheet costs Rs 8. What do 6 sticker sheets cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 48, because Rs 8 times 6 is Rs 48 in all

items.question: Rs 63 is shared equally by 3 friends. How much does each friend get?
items.final_answer: Rs 21 each, because Rs 63 divided by 3 is Rs 21 for each friend

items.question: At a fruit stall, oranges cost Rs 11 each and a melon costs Rs 46. A bill has 3 oranges and 1 melon. What is the total?
items.final_answer: Rs 79. Rs 11 times 3 is Rs 33 for the oranges, and Rs 33 plus Rs 46 is Rs 79 in all

items.question: A purse holds 1 note of Rs 50 and 3 coins of Rs 10. A pen set costs Rs 74. Is there enough money? How much is left or still needed?
items.final_answer: Yes. The purse holds Rs 80, and Rs 80 minus Rs 74 is Rs 6 left over

items.question: A class buys 9 museum tickets at Rs 26 each. What do all the tickets cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 234, because Rs 26 times 9 is Rs 234 in all

items.question: 8 notebooks cost Rs 192 in all, and every notebook has the same price. What does 1 notebook cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 24, because Rs 192 divided by 8 is Rs 24 for each notebook

items.question: A snack stall bill has 3 lines. 4 packets of biscuits cost Rs 23 each. 3 juice cartons cost Rs 19 each. 2 bags of nuts cost Rs 56 each. What is the total?
items.final_answer: Rs 261. Rs 23 times 4 is Rs 92 for the biscuits. Rs 19 times 3 is Rs 57 for the juice. Rs 56 times 2 is Rs 112 for the nuts. Rs 92 plus Rs 57 is Rs 149 so far, and Rs 149 plus Rs 112 is Rs 261 in all

items.question: A family has 1 note of Rs 500, 1 note of Rs 200, 2 coins of Rs 20 and 1 coin of Rs 5. They want 4 school bags. Each bag costs Rs 188. Is the money enough? How much more is needed or left?
items.final_answer: No. Rs 188 times 4 is Rs 752 in all. The money is Rs 745, and Rs 752 minus Rs 745 is Rs 7 more needed

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets how many things stand in the row, with a plus and a minus
lays the price tag out once for every thing in the row
opens a tray of money above a row of plates and deals it out equally
sets how many plates the money is shared between
swaps the shelf for a bill with a line for each thing and a total
stands a purse and a price tag on the two pans of a balance
types the cost, the share, the total and the difference

teaching_notes: Play the shop game with dummy notes and coins before the tool opens, and let the children price a few classroom things on paper. Ask each time whether the question wants the cost of many or the cost of one, and wait for the child to say which sum it is rather than saying it for them. Say Rs before every answer. In a bill, ask for the cost of each line before anyone adds anything. For the purse, count it aloud together first and compare it with the price second. If an answer is smaller than the price of one, ask whether many things can cost less than one. Use fresh prices: the printed bills and exercises are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a shop and bill tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A shelf at the left of the working area holds a row of one kind of thing with an amber price tag, and a sky blue count box with a plus and a minus sets how many. A Times button lays the price tag out once for every thing. A Share button opens a tray of money above a row of plates and deals it out equally. A Bill button swaps the shelf for a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule and a green Total. A Purse button stands a purse of notes and coins and a price tag on the two pans of a balance. Notes are plain flat rectangles in their own colour and coins plain round discs, each with its value in large type and nothing else on it. A words card says each step aloud and in writing. A green Answer tag holds what the child has typed. Each task sits at a small stall or shop. The number pad types the cost, the share, the total and the difference. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of things priced. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set how many things. Watch the price repeat. Share the money onto plates. Fill a bill and find the total. Count the purse and compare it with the price.
